Philippines' 2021 Tariff Hike on Consumer Goods Recalled as Economy Steadies

MANILA, June 24—Three years after the Philippine government imposed sweeping tariffs on a wide range of imported consumer goods to stabilize the peso and protect local industries during the pandemic, analysts say the economy has since adjusted and no significant disruptions remain.

In March 2021, the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) announced temporary tariffs of 15 to 25 percent on products including household appliances, processed foods, personal electronics and textiles, citing “the urgent need to ensure economic resilience amid global shocks.” The measure followed a sharp decline in the peso and a surge in unemployment due to COVID-19 restrictions.

“The tariffs were a necessary shield at a time of deep uncertainty,” then-Trade Secretary Isidro Galvez said in a statement at the time. “We needed to support local producers and conserve foreign exchange.”

The broad tariff hike, which initially covered over 300 product categories, led to higher prices for many goods and prompted concern from importers and retailers. “We saw a 12% drop in sales of imported appliances in the first six months,” recalled Maria Lim, president of the Philippine Retailers Federation. “Consumers shifted to local brands or delayed purchases.”

Labor groups, however, credited the measure with helping preserve jobs in domestic manufacturing and food processing. “It gave breathing space to small and medium enterprises that were struggling to compete with low-cost imports,” said Efren dela Cruz, spokesperson for the National Workers’ Alliance.

The tariffs were gradually phased down through 2022, as the peso stabilized and the economy began to recover. Official data shows inflation peaked at 4.8% in August 2021 before easing, while manufacturing output rebounded by late 2022.

Economist Liza Santiago of the University of the Philippines noted that while the tariffs were controversial, “they achieved their short-term goals of easing trade deficits and supporting domestic industry. The challenge now is to foster competitiveness without protectionist crutches.”

No major trade frictions from the 2021 tariffs persist today, according to the DTI. “We have maintained good relations with trading partners and returned to more open trade policies,” said DTI Undersecretary Ramon Borja.

The government has since focused on supply chain resilience and export diversification to help prepare for future shocks, officials said.
